title: Doubt in study
hookLine: doubt and questioning have always been part of Jewish study
tomorrow: Eli finally gets a whole line right. why does it taste like honey?

lines: THE TORAH HAS DOUBTERS IN IT.
cards: Some questions only come out in the back seat of a car, late, when nobody has to look at anybody. What if I'm not sure God is real? Can I still read the Torah?
Here is something worth hearing first. The Torah has doubters in it. Not in the footnotes.
In the story, out loud, with their names on it. And one of them argues with God, and at the end he's the one God praises.

teach.h: ABRAHAM: SHALL NOT THE JUDGE DO JUSTLY?
teach.b: Listen to their voices. Abraham hears that Sodom will be destroyed, and he doesn't bow and go quiet. He bargains.
He asks, in the JPS translation: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" He even says he is only dust and ashes, and keeps talking anyway.

The prophet Habakkuk opens his book with a complaint: "How long, O LORD, shall I cry, And Thou wilt not hear?" And Job. People say the patience of Job, but read the book: Job protests, for chapter after chapter.
His friends defend God with neat answers. At the end, God turns to one of those friends, Eliphaz, and says they have not spoken of Him the thing that is right, as His servant Job has.
The one who argued is the one who's praised. So doubt in study isn't a break from the tradition. It's one of its voices.
The Talmud calls a hard question a kushya, a difficulty, and the learning often starts right there.
Whether someone with doubts reads at a service is a question for their own community. But the text in front of them was not written by people who never wondered.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in the book of Job, the friends with the tidy answers are the ones God corrects.

how: In Jewish study, students are encouraged to raise a kushya, a hard question, and the books of Job and Habakkuk, with Abraham's plea for Sodom, are read as part of the tradition's own questioning.

games.q: in a study group, a friend says quietly, "honestly, i don't know if i believe any of this." the room goes silent. what fits the texts you just heard?
o: make room for it; Abraham and Job asked hard questions inside the story.
change the subject quickly so nobody feels uncomfortable.
explain why she's wrong, the way Job's friends did.
games.why: Abraham bargains, Habakkuk complains, Job protests, and it's the friends with neat answers whom God corrects.

practice: Say one doubt out loud, quietly, in plain words, the way Abraham spoke up. Then stay still and listen to the room for the rest of the sit: the hum of something electric, a car outside, your own breath.
The doubt was said, and the room is still here.

wordCard.voice: Doubt in study: the hard question spoken out loud, inside the learning, not outside it. Abraham, Habakkuk and Job all did it.

orig.note: Aramaic, in the Talmud: a difficulty, a hard question. where much of the learning starts.

carryVoice: The line for today: doubt is allowed; Abraham argued, and stayed in the conversation. See you soon.
